title: Can, want, must
goal: Use Norwegian's five helper verbs — and keep apart two phrases that sound alike but mean opposite things: *må ikke* and *trenger ikke*.
bekal: use *kan*, *vil*, *skal*, *må*, *bør* with the bare infinitive, without *å*
know that *må ikke* means **not allowed**, not "don't have to"
build longer sentences with two verbs at once
wave: Go back over **Unit 6** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Read all the numbers aloud again — especially *seksten*, *sytten* and *tjue*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Husreglene
dialogs.intro: Lars sticks a sheet of paper on the fridge door, then turns to Budi, who is making tea.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Du må lese husreglene før du flytter inn.
lines.id: You have to read the house rules before you move in.
lines.literal: you must read the-house-rules before you move in.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do I have to? Are they long?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Nei, bare fem punkter. Du kan lese dem på to minutter.
lines.id: No, just five points. You can read them in two minutes.
lines.literal: no, only five points. you can read them on two minutes.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Riktig. Og du må ikke spille musikk etter elleve.
lines.id: Right. And you mustn't play music after eleven.
lines.literal: right. and you must not play music after eleven.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vent. Betyr «må ikke» at jeg ikke har lov?
lines.id: Wait. Does *må ikke* mean I'm not allowed?
lines.literal: wait. means "must not" that I not have permission?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Nettopp. Hvis du bare slipper, sier vi «du trenger ikke».
lines.id: Exactly. If you just don't have to, we say *du trenger ikke*.
lines.literal: exactly. if you only are-let-off, say we "you need not".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Så «du må ikke vaske» og «du trenger ikke vaske» er helt forskjellige?
lines.id: So *du må ikke vaske* and *du trenger ikke vaske* are completely different?
lines.literal: so "you must not wash" and "you need not wash" are completely different?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Helt. Det første er forbudt, det andre er valgfritt.
lines.id: Completely. The first is forbidden, the second is optional.
lines.literal: completely. the first is forbidden, the other is optional.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Alle skal vaske kjøkkenet etter tur. Du bør begynne i kveld.
lines.id: Everyone cleans the kitchen in turn. You should start tonight.
lines.literal: all shall wash the-kitchen after turn. you should begin in evening.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Of course. Welcome to Norway, Budi.

notes: **Helper verbs don't end in -r.** *Jeg kan*, *du vil*, *han skal*, *vi må*, *de bør*. They're a group of their own, not irregulars — and once you know they never change at all, they become the easiest part of Norwegian.
**The verb that follows stands bare, without å**: *du må **lese***, not *du må å lese*. Exactly like English: "you must read", not "you must to read".

⚠️ **Here's the big trap. *Må ikke* means "must not", not "don't have to".** *Du må ikke røyke* = smoking is forbidden. If you mean "you don't have to smoke", the form is *du trenger ikke røyke*. Mixing them up can turn a ban into permission, and it's one of the most common mistakes newcomers make.
**Man** means "one, people" in a general sense — "one must not smoke", "we're not allowed". It's used just like formal English *one*, but far more often. The everyday alternative is *du*.
**Vil means "want", not "will".** English speakers trip hard here because *vil* looks like *will*. *Jeg vil* = "I want to". The future is handled by *skal*, and that's for Unit 17.
**Bør** means "should, ought to" — advice, not an order. It softens a sentence, and Norwegians use it a lot to avoid sounding pushy.

grammars.title: Five helper verbs
body: The present tense doesn't end in *-r* and never changes with the subject. The past tense is listed now so you'll recognize it when you meet it, although you'll only use it from Unit 15.
after: The last row doesn't fully belong to this group — *å få* still ends in *-r* — but it's used in exactly the same way: *får jeg komme inn?* (may I come in?). It's the most polite way to ask permission.

*Skal* and *må* can both come out as "have to" in English, but the difference is real: *må* means there's no choice (*jeg må jobbe* — or I'll be fired), while *skal* means it's scheduled or agreed (*jeg skal jobbe i morgen* — that's the plan).
*Kan* covers ability (*jeg kan svømme*) **and** permission (*kan jeg gå nå?*) **and** possibility (*det kan regne*). One word, three jobs — just like English *can*.

grammars.title: Two verbs in one sentence
body: The helper verb fills the second box, and the main verb is pushed out to the fifth box — past *ikke*. Watch how the sentence splits.
after: The last row shows one of the most useful expressions in Norwegian: **Skal vi…?** means "Shall we…?" / "How about we…?" — a polite and very common suggestion. *Skal vi gå?*, *Skal vi ta en kaffe?*
Notice that *ikke* stays loyally in the fourth box, and it's the main verb that jumps over it. If you're unsure, remember: **it's the second verb that moves, not *ikke***.

grammars.title: Må ikke versus trenger ikke
body: This page is worth bookmarking. Mixing up the following turns a ban into permission — and because *må* looks like "must" but is mostly used like "have to", it's easy to get wrong.
after: How to remember it: in *må ikke*, the negative hits the **action** — "you must: **not** smoke". In *trenger ikke*, it hits the **obligation** — "you don't: have to smoke".

Norwegian agrees with English *must not* here, and with German and Dutch too. The danger is translating *må* as "have to": *du må jobbe* = "you have to work", but *du må ikke jobbe* is never "you don't have to work" — it's "you mustn't work".

blocks.text: Norwegian has no everyday word that does the job of "please". Politeness is handled by **the form of the verb**, especially the past tense of the helper verbs — just as English uses *could* and *would*.

head: Norsk
English
How polite
rows: Can you pass me the salt?
Could you pass me the salt?
Could I have the salt, thanks?
polite, most common at the table

blocks.text: The phrase **vær så snill** ("be so kind") does exist and means "please", but Norwegians use it far less than English speakers use *please* — usually only when really pleading. Using it in every sentence actually sounds odd.

blocks.title: What you mustn't forget
items: *Takk* is used far more than *vær så snill*. For food: *takk for maten* (thanks for the food) is said every time you finish a meal at someone's home — skipping it is really noticed.
*Takk for sist* ("thanks for last time") is said when you meet someone again whom you last saw at a shared event. English has no equivalent, and Norwegians expect it.
*Vær så god* (**VÆR-seh-goo**) means "here you are" / "help yourself" — said when handing something over or inviting people to start eating.

sections.title: Eye training: one sentence, five helpers

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right. The content is the same; only how compulsory the action is changes.

head: Norsk
English
rows: I don't have to work tomorrow.
I'm not allowed to work tomorrow.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Pick one thing you'll do tomorrow. Say all eight sentences above with that activity, out loud.
Then turn them all into questions. Remember: it's the helper verb that moves to the front, not the main verb. *Må du jobbe i morgen?*
Finally, write five house rules for your own home in Norwegian — two with *må*, two with *må ikke*, one with *trenger ikke*.

vocab.en: a law; (ha lov) to be allowed

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right helper verb: *kan*, *vil*, *skal*, *må*, *bør*.
items: Jeg ____ svømme. Jeg lærte det som barn.
Jeg ____ jobbe i morgen — sjefen sa det.
Du ____ sove mer. Du ser trøtt ut.
Hva ____ du ha? Te eller kaffe?
I dag skal vi jobbe. → I dag ____
Vi trenger vaske i dag. → Vi ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: kan — Skal — skal — bør — vil — skal

I morgen må jeg jobbe. — Du må ikke røyke inne. — Skal vi ta en kaffe? — Jeg kan ikke komme. — Kan du hjelpe meg?
